questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish electron transfer bonding from electron pair sharing in a metal plus nonmetal reaction
questions.stem: A student heats magnesium powder with sulfur powder until the mixture glows brightly, and the white solid that forms dissolves in water. What holds the particles of this product together?

options.text: Electrostatic attraction between magnesium cations and sulfide anions in an extended array

options.misconception: treats a metal and a nonmetal as if they share pairs like two nonmetals do
options.text: Shared electron pairs between magnesium and sulfur atoms in separate molecules

options.misconception: assumes a metal plus a nonmetal always gives two-atom molecules
options.text: Shared electron pairs between magnesium and sulfur atoms in separate two-atom units

options.misconception: reads water solubility as proof of a hydrogen-bonded hydride solid
options.text: Hydrogen bonds between magnesium hydride and sulfide ions spread through the solid

questions.explanation: Magnesium is a metal and sulfur is a nonmetal, so this pair follows the transfer rule: magnesium loses two valence electrons to reach a neon configuration and sulfur gains them to reach an argon configuration. The resulting Mg2+ and S2- ions then feel Coulomb attraction to every oppositely charged neighbor, producing an extended array rather than separate molecules. The tempting wrong belief is that any two atoms joined in a formula must share electron pairs, but sharing is the rule only when two nonmetals bond.
questions.hint: Decide first whether the two elements are a metal with a nonmetal or two nonmetals.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state what a covalent bond is in terms of shared valence electrons
questions.stem: In hydrogen sulfide the sulfur and the two hydrogens are joined by covalent bonds. Which statement describes what actually holds each of those bonds together?

options.text: A shared pair of valence electrons pulled between two nonmetal atoms

options.misconception: applies the transfer rule to a pair that contains no metal at all
options.text: Electrons transferred from one metal atom to a nearby nonmetal atom

options.misconception: believes a shared pair must stay with one atom to count as a bond
options.text: A shared pair of valence electrons held entirely by one nonmetal atom

options.misconception: imports the metallic model into a molecular nonmetal compound
options.text: Delocalized valence electrons spread freely through a solid metal lattice

questions.explanation: The covalent rule is mutual sharing: two nonmetal atoms each contribute one electron to a pair that is then attracted to both nuclei, and that pair is the glue holding them at a fixed distance. Sulfur in H2S has six valence electrons and shares two of them, one with each hydrogen. The tempting wrong belief is that a bond requires full electron transfer, but a transferred electron creates an ion, not a shared pair between two nonmetal nuclei.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two atoms are both nonmetals that share rather than give away electrons.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: use the term formula unit for an ionic compound instead of molecule
questions.stem: A copy editor is revising a lab manual sentence about solid potassium sulfate. Which replacement states the particle situation correctly?

options.text: The formula unit, which gives the smallest whole-number ratio of the two ions

options.misconception: assumes an ionic ratio describes a discrete particle that exists alone
options.text: The molecule, which gives the exact count of ions inside each particle

options.misconception: keeps the right term but reinstates a separate countable particle
options.text: The formula unit, which gives the exact count of ions inside each particle

options.misconception: pairs the molecule term with the ratio idea, mixing the two models
options.text: The molecule, which gives the smallest whole-number ratio of the two ions

questions.explanation: A molecule is a discrete particle with a fixed atom count, which is the right word for a covalent substance such as water. In an ionic solid the ions are not grouped into separable particles, so the formula unit reports only the smallest whole-number ratio of cations to anions, here two potassium to one sulfate. The tempting wrong belief is that any stoichiometric formula represents a particle that can be pulled out of the solid intact, but that is the molecular model and it does not apply to a lattice.
questions.hint: Ask whether discrete countable particles exist in the solid, or only a repeating ratio.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: reject the idea that an ionic solid contains discrete two-ion molecules
questions.stem: A student insists that solid potassium chloride is made of separate KCl molecules packed tightly together. What does the ionic bonding model actually predict for one potassium ion?

options.text: It is attracted at once to every surrounding chloride ion, not just one

options.misconception: accepts the one-to-one pairing picture and only moves the pair in space
options.text: It is attracted only to the single chloride ion counted as its partner

options.misconception: switches to the covalent model while keeping the correct ion charges
options.text: It shares one electron pair with the chloride ion placed directly beside it

options.misconception: calls the ionic interaction a shared pair seen from the atom's view
options.text: It is bound to one chloride by a pair of electrons shared between both nuclei

questions.explanation: The bonding in an ionic solid is long-range Coulomb attraction, not a link to a chosen partner. Each K+ sits in a cavity surrounded by six chloride ions and each Cl- by six potassium ions, so every ion feels several opposite charges at once and the sum of those attractions makes the lattice rigid. The tempting wrong belief is that a formula ratio implies a discrete pair, but the pair picture leaves nothing holding distant neighbors together, so it cannot explain the high melting point or the shattering.
questions.hint: Ask how many opposite charges surround one ion in the array, not how many partners it has.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Charge balance in a formula unit
questions.learningObjective: derive the anion count needed for a cation from the ratio of ionic charges
questions.stem: Aluminum forms a 3+ cation and oxygen forms a 2- anion. How many oxide ions must combine with two aluminum ions to give a neutral compound?

options.misconception: assumes the two subscripts must always be equal to each other
multiplies the charges instead of matching their sum to zero
adds the two charge magnitudes to reach a subscript of six

questions.explanation: The rule is charge neutrality, so the total positive charge must cancel the total negative charge. Two Al3+ ions contribute 2 times 3, or plus 6, so six negative charges are needed, and since each oxide carries 2- that is three oxide ions, giving Al2O3. The tempting wrong belief is that the subscripts just repeat the two charge numbers, but charge magnitude is a tally to be balanced, not a count to be copied onto both sides of the formula.
questions.hint: Add up the charges on each side and require the total to equal zero.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: apply the octet rule to find how many bonds each carbon atom must form
questions.stem: In a stable neutral compound of carbon and hydrogen, every hydrogen holds two electrons and every carbon holds eight. How many bonds must each carbon form?

options.misconception: counts the octet as two electron pairs because an octet means eight pairs
applies the hydrogen duet to carbon as if carbon also needed two
confuses how many electrons carbon needs with how many it must share

questions.explanation: Carbon brings four valence electrons, so the octet rule means it must acquire four more, and in a neutral compound the only way to acquire electrons is to share them. Each shared pair adds exactly one electron to the carbon's count, so four bonds are needed, which is why carbon is always four-connected in a neutral hydrocarbon. The tempting wrong belief is that an octet means eight bonds, but an octet is eight electrons, and each bond supplies one of them to that carbon.
questions.hint: Count the electrons missing from the octet, not the electrons already present.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: count a double bond as a single electron domain
questions.stem: In carbon dioxide the central carbon is joined to 2 oxygen atoms by 2 double bonds and holds 0 lone pairs. How many electron domains does that carbon have?

options.misconception: counts the two bonding pairs of a double bond as separate directions
adds the two unfilled valence slots of carbon to the bonded directions
counts every shared electron pair instead of every direction from carbon

questions.explanation: The VSEPR rule counts directions of electron density, not electron pairs, and a multiple bond sits along one direction, so each C=O double bond contributes exactly one domain. Carbon has two such bonds and no lone pairs, giving 2 domains, a linear electron-domain geometry, and an ideal bond angle of 180 degrees. The tempting wrong belief is that two shared pairs mean two regions to push apart, but the four electrons of a double bond are pulled into one narrow zone and act as a single larger domain.
questions.hint: Count the regions of electron density around the atom, not the pairs inside them.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a tetrahedral domain geometry from a trigonal pyramidal shape
questions.stem: The central nitrogen in ammonia has 3 bonded hydrogen atoms and 1 lone pair, so it carries 4 electron domains. What is the molecular shape of ammonia?

options.text: trigonal pyramidal

options.misconception: reports the domain geometry and ignores the invisible lone pair
options.text: tetrahedral

options.misconception: counts only the three visible bonds and drops one domain from the count
options.text: trigonal planar

options.misconception: switches to a five-domain model no four-domain case can produce
options.text: trigonal bipyramidal

questions.explanation: The domain count is 3 bonds plus 1 lone pair, so the electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral with an ideal 109.5 degree angle, but the shape names only the atoms. One position is occupied by the lone pair instead of an atom, so the three hydrogens form a pyramid with nitrogen above their plane and the molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal. The tempting wrong belief is that shape equals domain geometry, but a lone pair counts for repulsion and is invisible when the shape is named from atoms.
questions.hint: Name the shape from the bonded atoms only, while counting all four domains for the angle.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Ideal angle from the domain count
questions.learningObjective: take the ideal bond angle from the domain count rather than the bonded-atom count
questions.stem: The central sulfur in sulfur dioxide has 2 bonded oxygen atoms and 1 lone pair, so it carries 3 electron domains. What is the ideal bond angle for that arrangement?

options.text: 120 degrees

options.misconception: copies the answer for a two-domain case instead of using three
options.text: 180 degrees

options.misconception: assumes a lone pair deletes a domain and drops the count to two
options.text: 109.5 degrees

options.misconception: borrows the right angle of a six-domain arrangement by mistake
options.text: 90 degrees

questions.explanation: The ideal angle belongs to the electron-domain geometry, and 3 domains settle in one plane 120 degrees apart to minimize repulsion. Sulfur's lone pair is the third domain, so the ideal O-S-O angle is 120 degrees even though only two atoms are bonded to sulfur and the molecule is drawn bent, because the shape is named from atoms while the angle is predicted from domains. The tempting wrong belief is that an angle follows the bonded-atom count, which gives 180 degrees here and drops the lone pair entirely.
questions.hint: Count every domain including the lone pair, then use the ideal angle for that count.

questions.learningObjective: predict a linear shape when a central atom has two domains and no lone pairs

options.text: tetrahedral

options.misconception: invents extra domains from unfilled valence positions in the atom
options.text: trigonal bipyramidal

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Lone pair compression of bond angles
questions.learningObjective: explain why a lone pair pushes an observed bond angle below the ideal domain angle
questions.stem: The H-N-H angle in ammonia is 107 degrees, with nitrogen holding 3 bonded hydrogens and 1 lone pair for 4 domains and an ideal 109.5 degrees. Nitrogen trifluoride also has 3 bonded fluorines and 1 lone pair, so what is the F-N-F angle?

options.text: 102.5 degrees

options.misconception: keeps the ammonia value by assuming only the central atom matters
options.text: 107.0 degrees

options.misconception: ignores the lone pair and reports the ideal angle as the real one
options.text: 109.5 degrees

options.misconception: assumes the more electronegative substituents push the bonds outward
options.text: 112.5 degrees

questions.explanation: Both molecules have 4 domains, so the ideal angle is 109.5 degrees in each, and in both the lone pair occupies more space than a bonding pair and squeezes the angle down. Fluorine is far more electronegative than hydrogen, so in NF3 each bonding pair is pulled away from nitrogen, the lone pair claims an even larger share of the room, and the angle shrinks past the ammonia value to about 102.5 degrees. The tempting wrong belief is that the lone pair is the only compressor, but the outer atoms change how much space each bond takes.
questions.hint: Both have four domains; ask what the more electronegative fluorines do to the bond pairs.

questions.learningObjective: predict a trigonal planar shape when a central atom has three domains and no lone pairs

options.text: trigonal pyramidal

options.misconception: borrows the four-domain model from a full octet on boron
options.text: tetrahedral

options.misconception: counts an extra domain from boron's empty valence position
options.text: trigonal bipyramidal

questions.learningObjective: read a described diagram of a four-domain molecule as tetrahedral
questions.stem: A diagram shows a central carbon atom in carbon tetrachloride with 4 single bonds drawn to 4 chlorine atoms at equal angles and 0 lone pairs on the carbon. What is the molecular shape shown by the diagram?

options.misconception: reads the flat drawing plane as the real arrangement of the atoms
options.text: trigonal planar

options.misconception: assumes one invisible lone pair is hiding behind the central carbon
options.text: trigonal pyramidal

options.misconception: switches to a six-domain model that the four bonds contradict

questions.learningObjective: read a six-domain molecule with two lone pairs opposite each other as square planar
questions.stem: A diagram shows the central xenon in xenon tetrafluoride with 4 bonded fluorine atoms and 2 lone pairs, for 6 electron domains in all. What is the molecular shape shown by the diagram?

options.misconception: counts six domains but reaches for a five-domain model

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: correct a domain miscount by recovering the T-shape for a five-domain molecule
questions.stem: A student counts 5 electron domains for the central chlorine in chlorine trifluoride, which has 3 bonded fluorine atoms and 2 lone pairs, then concludes the shape is trigonal planar because there are 3 bonds. Which shape does the domain count actually give?

options.text: T-shaped

options.misconception: repeats the student's error of counting bonds instead of domains
options.text: trigonal planar

options.misconception: assumes only one lone pair when the stem gives two
options.text: seesaw

options.misconception: reports the domain geometry instead of the shape left after removing
options.text: trigonal bipyramidal

questions.explanation: Three bonds plus two lone pairs is 5 domains, so the domain geometry is trigonal bipyramidal, whose ideal angles are 90 degrees between axial and equatorial and 120 degrees around the equator. The tempting wrong belief is that the shape follows the bonded-atom count, but the count that arranges the domains, not the count of visible bonds, decides the shape.

questions.learningObjective: predict a trigonal bipyramidal shape when a central atom has five domains and no lone pairs
questions.stem: The central phosphorus in phosphorus pentachloride has 5 bonded chlorine atoms and 0 lone pairs, so it carries 5 electron domains. What is the molecular shape of this compound?

options.misconception: assumes five directions must be coplanar around a central point

options.misconception: borrows the four-domain model because four is a familiar count
options.text: tetrahedral

options.misconception: assumes a lone pair is hiding on phosphorus with no basis

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Seesaw from five domains and one lone pair
questions.learningObjective: predict a seesaw shape when a five-domain central atom holds one lone pair
questions.stem: The central sulfur in sulfur tetrafluoride has 4 bonded fluorine atoms and 1 lone pair, so it carries 5 electron domains. What is the molecular shape of this compound?

options.text: seesaw

options.misconception: names the domain geometry and ignores the empty equatorial position
options.text: trigonal bipyramidal

options.misconception: assumes one lone pair fills the two axial slots as a pair
options.text: T-shaped

options.misconception: puts the lone pair on top of a four-domain model, not a five
options.text: square pyramidal

questions.explanation: Four bonds plus one lone pair is 5 domains, giving a trigonal bipyramidal domain geometry with ideal angles of 90, 120, and 180 degrees. A lone pair is bulkier than a bond, so it takes the one equatorial position, where it meets only two other domains at 120 degrees instead of the three 90 degree contacts an axial lone pair would have. That leaves two axial and two equatorial fluorines, and the tilted two-over-two arrangement is named a seesaw. The tempting wrong belief is that a lone pair always sits straight up and down, but axial is the crowded spot in a five-domain case.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two position types gives a lone pair fewer close contacts.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Unequal sharing in a polar covalent bond
questions.learningObjective: describe how a heteronuclear bond is shared unequally and which atom pulls harder
questions.stem: A bond is drawn between bromine and chlorine in bromine monochloride. How should the shared pair of valence electrons be distributed between the two atoms?

options.text: Unequally toward chlorine, which pulls the shared pair more strongly

options.misconception: assumes two halogens of the same group attract equally
options.text: Equally between the atoms, which pull with identical strength

options.misconception: makes atom size, not electronegativity, decide who wins the pair
options.text: Unequally toward bromine, which is the larger of the two

options.misconception: treats a small electronegativity gap as if it were an ionic transfer
options.text: Entirely onto bromine, which takes the pair as a full transfer

questions.explanation: When two different nonmetals bond, the more electronegative atom pulls the shared pair toward itself, and chlorine outranks bromine in the same group because it is higher and therefore better at pulling bonding electrons in. The unequal sharing makes bromine slightly positive and chlorine slightly negative without removing either electron, so the bond is polar covalent rather than ionic. The tempting wrong belief is that two atoms in the same group share equally, but electronegativity rises as you go up a group, so chlorine wins the pair.
questions.hint: Compare the electronegativity of the two halogens; do not rely on their size.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: sum bond dipoles as vectors to decide whether a molecule is polar
questions.stem: The central carbon in carbon dioxide has 2 bonded oxygen atoms joined by 2 double bonds and 0 lone pairs, so it has 2 electron domains at an ideal 180 degrees. Is carbon dioxide a polar molecule?

options.text: No, because its two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions

options.misconception: calls any molecule with a polar bond polar and ignores geometry
options.text: Yes, because each carbon-oxygen bond pulls charge toward its oxygen

options.misconception: believes linearity forbids polar bonds, not just net polarity
options.text: No, because a linear molecule can never contain polar bonds

options.misconception: compares two identical partial charges as if they did not match
options.text: Yes, because the two oxygens together outweigh the carbon's pull

questions.explanation: Two domains with no lone pairs force a 180 degree linear arrangement, so the two equal C=O bond dipoles are oriented directly opposite each other and their vector sum is zero, making the molecule nonpolar. Molecular polarity therefore depends on whether the bond dipoles cancel, not on whether any bond is polar. The tempting wrong belief is that a single polar bond makes the whole molecule polar, but that only holds when the geometry lets the dipoles add instead of cancelling.
questions.hint: Add the two bond dipoles as vectors before deciding anything.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state that dispersion forces act between every pair of particles
questions.stem: A textbook claims that nonpolar molecules such as dioxygen have no attractions between them at all. Which statement identifies what is wrong with that claim?

options.text: All particles have London dispersion, which grows with their electron count

options.misconception: calls the attractions permanent bonds even between separate molecules
options.text: Nonpolar molecules attract only through permanent bonds with each other

options.misconception: believes attractions belong only to polar species and vanish otherwise
options.text: Only polar molecules have any attraction between them at all

options.misconception: assumes dispersion needs a permanent dipole to be switched on
options.text: Dispersion needs a dipole, so it appears only in polar molecules

questions.explanation: London dispersion is present in every atom, ion, and molecule because a random fluctuation in its electron cloud briefly makes it dipolar and that instant dipole attracts the cloud of the next particle. Its strength scales with the number of electrons and the contact area, which is why dioxygen and iodine are both nonpolar yet differ enormously in boiling point. The tempting wrong belief is that nonpolar means non-attracting, but a nonpolar molecule still has a fluctuating dipole almost all the time.
questions.hint: Ask whether a temporary fluctuation could still make a dipole.

questions.learningObjective: read dipole moment as charge separation times distance across a data table
questions.stem: A table lists the four hydrogen halides with bond lengths HF 0.92, HCl 1.27, HBr 1.41, HI 1.61 angstroms, and dipole moments 1.82, 1.08, 0.82, and 0.44 debye in the same order. What relationship between the two columns does the data support?

options.text: Dipole moment falls as the bond length rises down the group

options.misconception: reads the two columns in the wrong direction against each other
options.text: Dipole moment rises as the bond length rises down the group

options.misconception: states the same trend as the keyed answer but in reversed words
options.text: Bond length falls as the dipole moment rises down the group

options.misconception: assumes one row covers four identical bonds and reads no trend
options.text: Both columns stay constant because all four bonds are identical

questions.explanation: A bond dipole is the partial charge times the distance over which that charge is separated, so as the halogen gets larger the H-X bond lengthens from 0.92 to 1.61 angstroms while the partial charges stay near 0.18, and the product dipole falls from 1.82 to 0.44 debye. The data therefore show dipole moment falling as bond length rises. The tempting wrong belief is that a heavier atom must be more polar because it is bigger, but size lengthens the bond while the charge separation itself barely changes.
questions.hint: Write each dipole as charge separation multiplied by bond distance.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: identify ion-dipole forces as the attraction that pulls an ion into water
questions.stem: When solid sodium chloride dissolves in water, what supplies the attraction that pulls the separated ions into solution?

options.text: Ion-dipole attractions between Na+ or Cl- and partial charges on water

options.misconception: credits ions with the hydrogen bonding that only water molecules do
options.text: Hydrogen bonds between Na+ or Cl- and the hydrogens in water

options.misconception: reduces an ion plus a polar molecule to a weak transient force
options.text: London dispersion forces between Na+ or Cl- and the water molecules

options.misconception: borrows the covalent picture for an ion meeting a neutral water molecule
options.text: Shared electron pairs between Na+ or Cl- and the oxygen in water

questions.explanation: Water is polar, so its oxygen end is slightly negative and its hydrogen ends slightly positive, and those permanent partial charges attract a full positive charge on Na+ and a full negative charge on Cl-. That ion-dipole attraction is strong because the charge on an ion is not a fraction, which is why salts dissolve well in water while neutral molecules of similar size do not. The tempting wrong belief is that only a full charge difference creates a strong attraction, but dipole fields scale with charge and it is a full charge on the ion.
questions.hint: Name the force between a full charge and a partial charge.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Formal charge and lone pairs in a polyatomic ion
questions.learningObjective: use the ion charge to decide whether the central atom keeps a lone pair
questions.stem: A student builds the Lewis structure of the ammonium ion, in which a central nitrogen carries a 1- missing electron, by making four nitrogen-hydrogen bonds to complete the octet. How many lone pairs remain on that nitrogen?

options.misconception: copies the lone pair of neutral ammonia onto the charged ion
counts the four bonds themselves as electron pairs to share
assumes four bonds means four nonbonding pairs as well

questions.explanation: Nitrogen brings 5 valence electrons, but the 1+ charge on the ion means one electron has been removed, leaving 4 to spend, and all 4 go into the four nitrogen-hydrogen bonds, so 8 electrons surround nitrogen and no lone pair is left. The tempting wrong belief is that nitrogen must keep a lone pair because the free atom has one, but the octet rule cares only about the total of 8 electrons around the atom, and four bonds supply all 8 by themselves.
questions.hint: Subtract the missing electron first, then spend what remains on bonds.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: correct a description that calls an ionic solid a lattice of shared-pair molecules
questions.practice: error analysis of a bonding model
questions.stem: A student writes that solid potassium oxide is made of two-atom molecules in which each potassium shares both of its valence electrons with one oxygen. Which statement corrects the bonding model while keeping the right ion charges?

options.text: Potassium transfers electrons to oxygen; the solid is an ion array, not molecules

options.misconception: repeats the sharing error and keeps the wrong particle picture intact
options.text: Potassium shares electrons with oxygen; the solid is a lattice of molecules

options.misconception: reverses which element loses the electrons, giving the wrong ion charges
options.text: Oxygen transfers electrons to potassium; the solid is an ion array, not molecules

options.misconception: fixes only the electron bookkeeping and leaves the wrong particle picture
options.text: Potassium transfers electrons to oxygen; the solid is a lattice of molecules

questions.explanation: Potassium is a metal and oxygen a nonmetal, so potassium loses one electron to reach an argon configuration and oxygen gains two to reach a neon configuration, giving K+ and O2- in a 2:1 ratio, and those ions attract every opposite-charge neighbor in an extended array rather than forming two-atom units. The tempting wrong belief is that a written formula represents a discrete molecule, but the two-atom picture survives the charge bookkeeping in two of the options and still fails, because nothing in an ionic lattice isolates a pair from its other neighbors.
questions.hint: Check the direction of electron movement and the particle picture separately.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: state metallic bonding as positive ions held by delocalized valence electrons
questions.stem: A teacher asks what specifically holds the atoms together inside a piece of copper. Which description gives the accepted metallic bonding model?

options.text: Positive metal ions held together by a sea of delocalized electrons

options.misconception: borrows the two-nonmetal sharing picture for a lattice of one element
options.text: Neutral metal atoms held together by shared pairs of valence electrons

options.misconception: reuses the alternating-charge lattice model for a single element
options.text: Positive and negative metal ions alternating in a regular crystal array

options.misconception: applies a molecular force to atoms that share no hydrogen at all
options.text: Neutral metal atoms held together by hydrogen bonds to nearby atoms

questions.explanation: A metal atom gives up its valence electrons, so the solid becomes an array of positive ion cores immersed in a cloud of those electrons, and the attraction between each ion core and the shared cloud is the metallic bond. That is why the same electrons can move through the whole piece instead of staying between two named atoms. The tempting wrong belief is that a bond must be a shared pair between two particular neighbors, but delocalization over the entire lattice is exactly what makes a metal a metal.
questions.hint: Ask what a metal atom does with its valence electrons in the solid.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Valence electrons in the delocalized sea
questions.learningObjective: infer the number of delocalized electrons from the charge on a metal cation
questions.stem: In solid magnesium every atom has become an ion with a 2+ charge, and each of those donated valence electrons now moves freely through the metal. How many valence electrons did each magnesium atom contribute?

options.misconception: picks the group number instead of the count of electrons actually given up
assumes the ion gained electrons instead of losing them to the sea
adds the nuclear charge to the valence count to reach twelve

questions.explanation: The 2+ charge on the magnesium ion is itself the record of the transfer, because an ion that ends up two positive has given up exactly two electrons, and those two are the valence electrons that now wander through the delocalized sea. Magnesium is in group 2, so two donated electrons is also the valence count. The tempting wrong belief is that the group number is the electron count, but group 2 gives two valence electrons while the total in the atom is twelve, and only the two outermost ones are delocalized.
questions.hint: The charge on the ion tells you how many electrons left the atom.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: reject a localized-pair explanation of metallic conduction
questions.practice: error analysis of a bonding explanation
questions.stem: A student explains the electrical conductivity of copper by saying each atom is joined to its neighbors by localized two-center two-electron bonds, and the current flows because those bonds break and release their electrons. What is the error in that explanation?

options.text: Metallic bonding is not localized pairs; valence electrons are delocalized

options.misconception: keeps the localized-pair model and attacks the identity of the neighbors
options.text: Metallic bonds do hold two electrons, but the neighbors are not all copper

options.misconception: keeps the localized-pair model and denies that electrons can ever move
options.text: Localized electron pairs are right, but no charge can move through a solid

options.misconception: keeps the localized-pair model and reinvents an alternating ion lattice
options.text: Metallic bonding is not localized pairs; the atoms are neutral and separate

questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is a single system in which the valence electrons are delocalized over the whole lattice and the positive ion cores are held by their attraction to that shared cloud, so an applied field already has mobile electrons available to drift without any bond breaking. The tempting wrong belief is that conduction requires bonds to break, but in a metal no bond breaks at all, because the electrons were never confined to a pair between two named atoms in the first place.
questions.hint: Ask whether the electrons were ever confined to a pair between two atoms.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.topic: Boiling points across a dispersion series
questions.learningObjective: explain a rising boiling point across an alkane series as growing dispersion
questions.stem: A table lists four alkanes with molar masses and boiling points: methane at 16.0 grams per mole boils at -161.5 degrees Celsius, ethane at 30.1 boils at -88.6, propane at 44.1 boils at -42.1, and butane at 58.1 boils at -0.5. By how many degrees Celsius does the last-listed alkane boil above the first-listed one?

options.text: 161.0 degrees Celsius

options.misconception: subtracts the two middle rows instead of the two ends of the table
options.text: 46.5 degrees Celsius

options.misconception: adds the absolute values of both boiling points instead of taking the rise
options.text: 162.0 degrees Celsius

options.misconception: swaps the two endpoints and computes the change in the other direction
options.text: 175.5 degrees Celsius

questions.explanation: All four are nonpolar, so the only intermolecular force available is London dispersion, and dispersion strength rises with polarizability, so the climb from 16.0 to 58.1 grams per mole tracks the rise in boiling point. The last-listed value of -0.5 degrees minus the first-listed value of -161.5 degrees is a rise of 161.0 degrees Celsius. The tempting wrong belief is that a hydrocarbon series shows hydrogen bonding, but no alkane has a hydrogen on nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine, so the whole trend is dispersion.
questions.hint: Take the difference of the two boiling points, then check which force fits.
